result.summary: The Ghost of Clytaemestra rouses the sleeping Furies, who wake furious that Orestes has escaped. Apollo drives them from his shrine, and they argue over whether killing a mother is worse than killing a husband. The scene then moves to Athens, where Orestes clasps Athena's image and awaits judgment.

scenes.title: The Ghost Wakes the Furies
scenes.summary: Clytaemestra's ghost urges the sleeping Furies to hunt Orestes. They wake, find him gone, and accuse Apollo of theft and pollution.
scenes.stakes: The Furies risk losing their quarry, and Clytaemestra's wrong stays unavenged.

scenes.title: Apollo Confronts the Furies
scenes.summary: Apollo orders the Furies out of his shrine. They debate their duties, matricide against killing a husband, and he sends the case to Athena. Both depart, and Apollo vows to protect Orestes.
scenes.stakes: Apollo's honor as protector of his suppliant, and the Furies' ancient privileges, are both at risk.

scenes.title: Orestes Seeks Athena
scenes.summary: Hermes brings Orestes to Athens, where he embraces Athena's image and waits for his trial.
scenes.stakes: Orestes' life and freedom from the Furies depend on the goddess's judgment.

alias_notes.explanation: A title of Apollo as oracular god.
Title of the love goddess, from Cyprus.

notable_quotes.reason: Apollo argues marriage bond is mightier than an oath, with Justice as guardian.
The Furies voice the clash between older and younger gods.

analysis.text: The scene stages the conflict between old blood-vengeance and the new order of Olympian justice.
Moving the action to Athens prepares for the founding of the Areopagus court, which Aeschylus presents as the city's civic institution.

language_notes.text: The Furies are likened to dreaming hounds whimpering as they chase prey in sleep; 'game' means the quarry, Orestes.
'Prelude' refers to the ghost's urging, a preliminary warning; 'aught in vain' means anything useless.
'Sooth' means truly, in truth.
'Toils' are hunting nets; the image continues the Furies' role as hounds hunting Orestes.
A 'goad' is a pointed stick used to drive animals, here wielded like a charioteer's.
'Doomster' means one who pronounces judgment or doom; here the scourge of the avenging reproach.
The 'centre-stone' is the omphalos at Delphi, believed to mark the earth's center and Apollo's shrine.
'Eld' means old age or ancient times; 'apportionments of eld' are the ancient divine allotments of honors and powers.
"Avaunt" is an archaic command meaning "be gone!" or "get away from here!"
"Smitten by a winged glistering snake" refers to Apollo's golden arrows, imagined as flying serpents; "spume" is foam or froth.
"Meet" means fitting or suitable; "in sooth" means truly.
"Abettor" means one who aids or encourages a crime; the Furies say Apollo is the real author of the killing.
"Red-handed" means stained with fresh blood; "engage thyself" means you pledged yourself.
"Expiation" is ritual purification or atonement for a crime such as murder.
"Forsooth" is an archaic, here sarcastic, word for "indeed."
"In good sooth" means "truly"; "pledges" are the marriage vows that Hera and Zeus guard as gods of marriage.
Cypris is Aphrodite, named for Cyprus; she presides over love and desire, hence over the union of man and woman.
"’Twixt" is "betwixt", meaning between. Apollo argues that the marriage bond, guarded by Justice, outweighs any sworn oath.
"Takest it sore to heart" means you take it very seriously; "remiss in act" means careless in action. He accuses her of inconsistency.
"Him who seeketh purification" is the suppliant Orestes; Apollo says abandoning him would bring terrible divine anger.
Orestes says his guilt's "edge" is blunted by time and travel, meaning the pollution of his crime has worn down through ritual purification and wandering.

context_notes.text: Zeus's son is Apollo, who had sheltered Orestes at Delphi and purified him after the murder of Clytaemestra.
The Furies are older goddesses, daughters of Night, who see the Olympian gods such as Apollo as upstart younger deities.
The conflict between older and younger gods is central to the play.
Apollo, god of prophecy, owns the Delphic shrine where Orestes has taken refuge; the Furies, who pursue murderers, have followed him inside and fallen asleep.
Apollo had commanded Orestes to kill his mother Clytemnestra to avenge her murder of his father Agamemnon.
Hera, the Fulfiller (Teleia), presided over marriage. Zeus and Hera were the divine model of the marriage bond.
Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom and patron of Athens, will judge the case, which leads to the founding of the Areopagus court.
Embracing the god's image made a suppliant sacred; he could not be seized without offending the deity.
Loxias is a title of Apollo as prophetic god. Orestes was ordered by his oracle to go to Athens and Athena.

literary_notes.text: Fourfold repetition imitates urgent hunting cries and the Furies' muttering in sleep.
The sleeping Furies are compared to dogs, stressing their animal, relentless pursuit.
The sting of reproach is compared to a charioteer's goad, making the ghost's words physically painful.
The blood-dripping throne is a vivid image accusing the younger gods of rule built on pollution.
A catalogue of gruesome tortures paints the Furies' world as one of violence and pollution, set against Apollo's clean shrine.
Likening the Furies to beasts in a lion's den dehumanizes them and stresses their bloodthirst and impurity.
Calling the Furies a "herd without a shepherd" mocks them as lawless creatures that no god guides or claims.
Rapid one-line exchanges between Apollo and the Chorus sharpen the quarrel and expose each side's argument.
Apollo turns the Furies' argument against them by presenting Cypris as a wronged deity, showing him as a skilled, partisan debater.
The Chorus's repeated, defiant "never, never" shows their single-minded, relentless nature as pursuers.
Apollo stresses the suppliant's wrath as "appalling in heaven and on earth," raising the stakes of his promise to protect Orestes.
Orestes addresses the absent goddess directly as "O goddess," making his plea a formal prayer.
